newsitem.title: USA: Fears on IRS yield burning ruling overblown-lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Fears on IRS yield burning ruling overblown-lawyer.

text.p: Fears over the U.S. Internal Revenue Service's response to "yield burning" in the municipal bond market is "overblown," a prominent bond lawyer told 1,000 of his colleagues meeting here on Thursday.

"The amnesty program is such a dumb idea, that as soon as it came out I decided to ignore it," Richard Chirls, a partner with Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe in New York, said in a keynote speech at the National Association of Bond Lawyers annual workshop.

Chirls was referring to a July 19 IRS ruling that gives issuers of advance refunding bonds the option of entering into "closing agreements" with IRS to head off possibly having interest on their bonds declared taxable.

Municipalities would have to agree to pay the Treasury the difference between the price they paid and the spot price of the securities on the purchase date, plus interest on that figure under the IRS procedure, which triggered a howl of protest from municipalities nationwide.

IRS yesterday announced it was extending the one-year deadline for entering closing agreements indefinitely while it reviews the controversial procedure. But it did not suspend the ruling, disappointing many of the bond lawyers meeting here this week.
Chirls said he did not see investment bankers "marching to Washington to fess up to their sins" in response to the closing agreement program.

He added that issuers "have to recognize that if they go to Washington they have to bring a check with them. And they are not going to want to bring that check unless it is backed up with the support of the people who participated in the transaction.
"And that joint contribution to the federal (government) is just not going to happen," Chirls said.
"So, I just don't think there's much going on here to get too excited about," Chirls said. He said the yield burning controversy will trigger extensive litigation by issuers against dealers.
"The train to the 21st century will be a litigious one" for municipal market participants, Chirls said.
On another front burner issue, Chirls criticized U.S. Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan's (D-NY) bill to bar the use of tax exempt bonds for stadium financings.
"This is a bad idea Senator Moynihan," Chirls said.

"It's federal meddling into areas that are a local affair. If municipalities can choose between building a school, or roadway or city hall using tax exempt bonds, they also should have the choice of spending their own money to build professional sports stadiums even if they benefit professional teams," Chirls said.
Chirls said Moynihan's bill has pitted two elements of the municipal bond community against each other.

"You now have the university people who will develop the arguments for how bad sports stadium financing is. And then you have the city folk and sports people telling how bad the university financings are," Chirls said.
"We really don't need our own people developing the arguments for why what we do is bad," Chirls said.
